It sets the highest usable QAM order. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="estimator"></a>**Estimator** — A rule for computing a parameter's value from data, such as the sample mean; the result, an estimate, is itself a random variable with a sampling distribution. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="eulers-formula"></a>**Euler's formula** — e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ for real θ. It connects exponentials and sinusoids and makes r∠θ and re^{jθ} the same number. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="eulers-method"></a>**Euler's method** — The simplest numerical ODE solver, y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n); first-order accurate, and on y' = −y/τ stable only for steps h < 2τ. Its implicit (backward) form is stable for any step. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="exception"></a>**Exception** — An object signalling an error that stops normal execution until handled by try/except; raising one with a clear message is how code refuses invalid input instead of returning a wrong value. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="existence-and-uniqueness-theorem"></a>**Existence and uniqueness theorem** — A linear first-order IVP with continuous coefficients has exactly one solution on the whole interval of continuity; a nonlinear one y' = f(t, y) has a unique local solution when f and ∂f/∂y are continuous (Picard–Lindelöf). *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="expectation"></a>**Expectation** — The probability-weighted average of a random variable, Σ k·p(k) or ∫ x·f(x) dx; its long-run average over many independent trials, also called the mean. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="exponential-distribution"></a>**Exponential distribution** — The waiting time to the first event of a Poisson process with rate r, P(T > t) = e^(−rt), with mean 1/r; the model behind constant failure rates. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Memoryless property](#memoryless-property), [FIT (failures in time)](#fit-failures-in-time).

<a id="exponential-function"></a>**Exponential function** — The function eˣ (e ≈ 2.71828), whose rate of change equals its value; physical decays are written y₀e^(−t/τ) with time constant τ. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md). *See also:* [Natural logarithm](#natural-logarithm), [Half-life](#half-life).

<a id="exponential-response-formula"></a>**Exponential response formula** — For p(D)y = e^{st} with p(s) ≠ 0, a particular solution is y = e^{st}/p(s); when s is a simple root of p, y = t e^{st}/p'(s) instead (the resonant case). *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="letter-f"></a>

## F

<a id="fabless"></a>**Fabless** — A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to foundries (and assembly and test to OSATs). *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md). *See also:* [Foundry](#foundry).

<a id="faraday-cage"></a>**Faraday cage** — A closed conducting enclosure; its empty interior has zero electrostatic field whatever the outside charges, and it shields both ways only when grounded. Seams, apertures and low-frequency magnetic fields limit real shields. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="faradays-law"></a>**Faraday's law** — The EMF around a closed loop equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through it, ℰ = −N dΦ/dt; changing flux makes the electric field non-conservative, so voltage then depends on the path. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md). *See also:* [Lenz's law](#lenzs-law).

<a id="fastspice"></a>**FastSPICE** — A class of transistor-level circuit simulators that partition the circuit and use simplified or tabulated device models to gain speed and capacity, at some loss of accuracy relative to SPICE. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [SPICE](#spice).

<a id="fault-coverage"></a>**Fault coverage** — The fraction of modeled faults (for example stuck-at faults) that a set of test patterns detects. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md). *See also:* [Defect level (DPPM)](#defect-level-dppm).

<a id="fermi-energy"></a>**Fermi energy** — The highest occupied electron energy at absolute zero, E_F = (ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^(2/3) for a free-electron gas (about 7 eV in copper); at finite temperature the Fermi level is the energy whose occupation probability is one half. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="fermi-estimate"></a>**Fermi estimate** — An order-of-magnitude estimate built from rounded assumptions and simple multiplication, used to sanity-check calculations and claims. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="fermi-dirac-distribution"></a>**Fermi–Dirac distribution** — The probability f(E) = 1/(1 + e^((E − E_F)/kT)) that an electron state of energy E is occupied in equilibrium; it falls from 0.9 to 0.1 over about 4.4 kT and reduces to the Boltzmann factor far above E_F. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="ferromagnetism"></a>**Ferromagnetism** — Strong, spontaneous alignment of atomic magnetic moments in domains (iron, nickel, cobalt, ferrites), giving high permeability, saturation and hysteresis. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="final-value-theorem"></a>**Final-value theorem** — f(∞) = lim sF(s) as s → 0, valid only if f actually settles, that is, every pole of sF(s) lies in the open left half-plane; applied to an unstable or oscillating signal it gives a wrong answer. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Initial-value theorem](#initial-value-theorem), [DC gain](#dc-gain).

<a id="finite-time-blow-up"></a>**Finite-time blow-up** — A solution of a nonlinear ODE reaching infinity at a finite time although the equation is smooth, as for y' = y² with y = 1/(1 − t); it signals superlinear positive feedback. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="first-order-circuit"></a>**First-order circuit** — A circuit whose behavior is described by a first-order differential equation, typically one with a single (equivalent) capacitor or inductor. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="first-silicon-success"></a>**First-silicon success** — A chip's first manufactured version (A0) being functionally correct and shippable without a respin; reported for a minority of IC/ASIC projects in industry surveys. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="fit-failures-in-time"></a>**FIT (failures in time)** — A failure rate of one failure per 10^9 device-hours; soft-error rates of memories are quoted in FIT per megabit. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="fixed-point-arithmetic"></a>**Fixed-point arithmetic** — Representing fractions as integers with an agreed scale 2^−f, so integer hardware does the arithmetic; additions are direct, products must be rescaled, and rounding, overflow and saturation are managed by the programmer. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md). *See also:* [Q format](#q-format), [Saturation arithmetic](#saturation-arithmetic).

<a id="flicker-1-f-noise"></a>**Flicker (1/f) noise** — Noise whose power spectral density falls as 1/f, so every decade of frequency carries equal power; dominant at low frequencies in MOSFETs. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="floating-point-number"></a>**Floating-point number** — A number stored as sign, exponent and fraction in binary; IEEE 754 binary64 (Python float, C double) has 53 significant bits (about 16 decimal digits), so most decimals such as 0.1 are approximated. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="floor-division"></a>**Floor division** — Division that rounds the quotient down toward minus infinity (Python's //), paired with a remainder (%) that takes the divisor's sign; −7 // 2 is −4 in Python but C's integer division gives −3. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="flux"></a>**Flux** — The surface integral of a vector field's normal component, ∬ F · dA, measuring how much of the field passes through a surface. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="flyback-diode"></a>**Flyback diode** — A diode placed across an inductive load so that, when the driving switch opens, the inductor's current circulates through the diode, clamping the switch voltage to about one diode drop above the supply. Also called a freewheeling diode. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="force-voltage-analogy"></a>**Force–voltage analogy** — The mapping of a mass–spring–damper onto a series RLC circuit (force ↔ voltage, velocity ↔ current, mass ↔ L, damping ↔ R, compliance 1/k_s ↔ C); it turns mechanical systems into circuits that SPICE can simulate. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="form-factor"></a>**Form factor** — RMS value divided by the rectified average; π/(2√2) ≈ 1.111 for a sine. Average-responding meters assume this value. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="formal-verification"></a>**Formal verification** — Using mathematical proof (model checking, equivalence checking) to show that a design satisfies a property for all possible inputs, instead of testing examples. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="forward-error-correction-fec"></a>**Forward error correction (FEC)** — Adding redundant symbols so the receiver can correct errors without retransmission; it lets links run at a raw BER near 1e-4 and still deliver 1e-13 or better. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="foster-network"></a>**Foster network** — An RC model written as a series chain of parallel R–C pairs, Z(t) = Σ Rᵢ(1 − e^(−t/τᵢ)); it is a modal (eigenvalue) expansion whose nodes have no physical meaning, so it cannot be cascaded with other stages. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="foundry"></a>**Foundry** — A company that manufactures chips designed by its customers, supplying them with a process and its PDK. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="fourier-coefficient"></a>**Fourier coefficient** — The amplitude of one harmonic in a periodic signal, b_n = (2/T)∫ x(t) sin(nωt) dt (and a_n with cosine), found by orthogonality. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="fowler-nordheim-tunneling"></a>**Fowler–Nordheim tunneling** — Tunneling through a triangular barrier formed when a strong field tilts an insulator's band; the current rises steeply with field (about seven orders of magnitude from 7 to 10 MV/cm in SiO₂) and is used to program and erase flash. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="frequency-response"></a>**Frequency response** — The complex gain H(jω) of a linear system at angular frequency ω. Its magnitude scales a sinusoid's amplitude and its angle shifts the sinusoid's phase. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Corner frequency](#corner-frequency).

<a id="fubinis-theorem"></a>**Fubini's theorem** — For well-behaved integrands, a double integral can be evaluated as two nested single integrals in either order; reversing the order can turn an impossible integral into an easy one. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Double integral](#double-integral).

<a id="function"></a>**Function** — A rule that assigns exactly one output to each allowed input; in engineering both input and output usually carry units (for example voltage as a function of time). *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md). *See also:* [Domain and range](#domain-and-range), [Inverse function](#inverse-function).

<a id="function-prototype"></a>**Function prototype** — A C declaration giving a function's name, return type and parameter types without its body, so that other translation units can call it; usually placed in a header file. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="functional-coverage"></a>**Functional coverage** — A measure of which specified behaviors, input combinations or corner cases a verification run has actually exercised; used to decide when verification is complete. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="fundamental-theorem-of-calculus"></a>**Fundamental theorem of calculus** — Part 1, the accumulated area ∫_a^x f has derivative f(x); part 2, ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F. Integration and differentiation are inverse operations. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md).

<a id="letter-g"></a>

## G

<a id="gauge-factor"></a>**Gauge factor** — The ratio of a strain gauge's fractional resistance change to the strain, GF = (ΔR/R)/ε; about 2 for metal-foil gauges. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="gausss-law"></a>**Gauss's law** — The electric flux out of any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀; with symmetry it gives fields of spheres, lines and planes in one line. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Divergence theorem](#divergence-theorem).

<a id="gaussian-distribution"></a>**Gaussian distribution** — The normal (bell-curve) distribution with density e^(−(x−μ)²/(2σ²))/(σ√(2π)); thermal noise and sums of many independent small effects follow it. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Q-function](#q-function).

<a id="gaussian-elimination"></a>**Gaussian elimination** — Solving Ax = b by subtracting multiples of rows to reach an upper-triangular system, then back-substituting; it costs about (2/3)n³ flops for an n×n system. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md). *See also:* [Pivot](#pivot), [LU factorization](#lu-factorization).

<a id="gaussian-surface"></a>**Gaussian surface** — An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law, ideally one on which the field is constant and perpendicular (or parallel, carrying no flux), such as a sphere, coaxial cylinder or pillbox. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="geometric-distribution"></a>**Geometric distribution** — The number of independent trials up to and including the first success, with PMF (1 − q)^(k−1) q; it is memoryless. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="geometric-series"></a>**Geometric series** — Σ a r^k, which sums to a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1 and diverges otherwise; models reflections, feedback loops, digital filters and annuities. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="gibbs-phenomenon"></a>**Gibbs phenomenon** — The persistent overshoot, about 9 % of the jump, of truncated Fourier series near a discontinuity; it narrows but does not shrink as harmonics are added. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="gradient"></a>**Gradient** — The vector of partial derivatives ∇f; it points in the direction of steepest increase, its length is that steepest rate, and it is perpendicular to level curves. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="gradient-descent"></a>**Gradient descent** — Minimizing a function by repeated steps x ← x − η∇f; stable only for step sizes below 2 divided by the largest curvature, and slow when the condition number is large. The workhorse of neural-network training. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="grounding"></a>**Grounding** — Connecting a conductor to a large charge reservoir (the earth or a circuit's ground plane) that can supply or absorb charge freely, fixing its potential and draining the charge induced on its outer surface. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="letter-h"></a>

## H

<a id="half-life"></a>**Half-life** — The time for an exponentially decaying quantity to halve, τ ln 2 ≈ 0.693τ; for growth the same expression is the doubling time. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="half-power-bandwidth"></a>**Half-power bandwidth** — The width ω₂ − ω₁ of the band over which a resonant response stays within 1/√2 of its peak (half the power); for a second-order band-pass it equals ω₀/Q exactly, with ω₁ω₂ = ω₀². *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md). *See also:* [Quality factor](#quality-factor).

<a id="hall-effect"></a>**Hall effect** — The transverse voltage V_H = IB/(nqt) across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field; its sign gives the carrier type and its size the carrier density, and semiconductor Hall plates make magnetic sensors. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="hardware-description-language-hdl"></a>**Hardware description language (HDL)** — A language such as Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL for describing digital hardware structure and behavior, used for simulation and synthesis. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="harmonic-distortion"></a>**Harmonic distortion** — Output at integer multiples of an input sinusoid's frequency, produced by nonlinearity; HD2 ≈ (a₂/2a₁)A and HD3 ≈ (a₃/4a₁)A² from the Taylor coefficients. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md). *See also:* [Total harmonic distortion (THD)](#total-harmonic-distortion-thd).

<a id="harmonic-series"></a>**Harmonic series** — Σ 1/k, which diverges (slowly, like ln n) even though its terms shrink to zero. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="hash-table"></a>**Hash table** — A key-value store that computes each key's array slot with a hash function, giving O(1) average lookup; collisions are resolved by chaining or open addressing, and the table resizes as its load factor grows. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md). *See also:* [Load factor](#load-factor).

<a id="hazard-rate"></a>**Hazard rate** — The failure rate among survivors, h(t) = f(t)/R(t); constant for the exponential, falling for infant mortality, rising for wear-out. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="header-file"></a>**Header file** — A C file (.h) of declarations (prototypes, types, macros) that a module offers, included by its users; wrapped in an include guard so its contents are processed once per translation unit. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="heap-memory"></a>**Heap (memory)** — The region for dynamic allocation (malloc, calloc, realloc, free), whose blocks live until freed; flexible in size but subject to leaks, fragmentation and unpredictable allocation time. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="hessian"></a>**Hessian** — The matrix of second partial derivatives of a function; its determinant and signs classify critical points as minima, maxima or saddles. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="hidden-state"></a>**Hidden state** — Values held in a notebook kernel's memory that the visible code, read top to bottom, does not explain (from deleted, edited or out-of-order cells); cured by restarting the kernel and running all cells. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="high-k-dielectric"></a>**High-k dielectric** — An insulator with permittivity well above SiO₂'s 3.9 (HfO₂ and ZrO₂ about 25), used in transistor gates and DRAM capacitors to get high capacitance from a physically thicker, less leaky film. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="hole"></a>**Hole** — An empty state near the top of an otherwise full valence band, which carries current as a positive charge with positive effective mass; holes are the carriers of p-type silicon and PMOS transistors. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="homogeneity"></a>**Homogeneity** — Scaling property of a linear system, f(a x) = a f(x); in a circuit with one source, every response is proportional to the source. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Linearity](#linearity), [Unit-output method](#unit-output-method).

<a id="htol"></a>**HTOL** — High-temperature operating life test; JEDEC JESD47G (2009) specifies at least 125 °C junction temperature for 1000 h on 3 lots of 77 units with zero failures (the HTOL row of the current revision, Rev N listed Aug 2026, was not checked). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="human-body-model-hbm"></a>**Human-body model (HBM)** — The component ESD test of ANSI/ESDA/JEDEC JS-001, modeling a charged person as 100 pF discharged through 1.5 kΩ (peak current 0.667 A per kV); the industry-recommended qualification target is 1 kV. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="hyperbolic-functions"></a>**Hyperbolic functions** — cosh x = (e^x + e^−x)/2, sinh x = (e^x − e^−x)/2 and tanh = sinh/cosh, linked by cosh² − sinh² = 1; they describe catenaries, overdamped responses, transmission-line input impedance and the differential pair's tanh transfer curve. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="hypothesis-test"></a>**Hypothesis test** — A decision rule that rejects a null hypothesis when data would be sufficiently unlikely under it, with a stated significance level α (false-alarm probability). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="hysteresis-magnetic"></a>**Hysteresis (magnetic)** — The dependence of a ferromagnet's B on its magnetic history, traced as a B–H loop; soft materials (cores) have narrow loops, hard materials (permanent magnets) wide ones. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="letter-i"></a>

## I

<a id="iq"></a>**I/Q (in-phase/quadrature)** — Representation of a bandpass signal by two baseband components, in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q), which together form one complex sample stream I + jQ; the native signal format of modern radios. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Error vector magnitude](#error-vector-magnitude).

<a id="ideal-current-source"></a>**Ideal current source** — An element that maintains a specified current regardless of the voltage across it; a 0 A source is an open circuit. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Ideal voltage source](#ideal-voltage-source).

<a id="ideal-voltage-source"></a>**Ideal voltage source** — An element that maintains a specified voltage between its terminals regardless of the current through it; a 0 V source is a short circuit. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Ideal current source](#ideal-current-source), [Internal resistance](#internal-resistance).

<a id="illusion-of-competence"></a>**Illusion of competence** — The mistaken feeling of mastery produced by recognizing familiar material (for example, while re-reading a solution), as opposed to being able to recall and apply it unaided. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="imaginary-unit"></a>**Imaginary unit** — The number j defined by j² = −1 (written i in mathematics; EE uses j because i denotes current). Multiplying by j rotates a complex number 90° counterclockwise. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="impedance"></a>**Impedance** — The ratio Z = V/I of voltage phasor to current phasor for an element or network, in ohms. Resistor R, inductor jωL, capacitor 1/(jωC). *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Reactance](#reactance), [Phasor](#phasor).

<a id="impedance-of-free-space"></a>**Impedance of free space** — η₀ = √(µ₀/ε₀) ≈ 376.7 Ω, the ratio E/H in a plane wave in vacuum; η₀/√ε_r in a dielectric. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="implicit-differentiation"></a>**Implicit differentiation** — Differentiating both sides of an equation that defines y in terms of x, treating y as a function of x; used to differentiate ln x, arctan x and curves such as circles. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="improper-integral"></a>**Improper integral** — An integral over an infinite interval or of an unbounded integrand, defined as a limit; it converges if the limit is finite (for example ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges only for p > 1). *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="impulse"></a>**Impulse** — The time integral of force, J = ∫F dt (N·s), equal to the change in momentum; a short, violent impact and a longer, gentler stop can carry the same impulse. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="impulse-response"></a>**Impulse response** — h(t), a system's output when the input is δ(t) with zero initial conditions; its transform is the transfer function, and the output for any input is the convolution h \* x. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Convolution](#convolution), [Transfer function](#transfer-function).

<a id="incidence-matrix"></a>**Incidence matrix** — The branch-by-node matrix of a circuit graph, with +1 at each branch's start node and −1 at its end node. Its rank is n − 1 for a connected graph, the conductance matrix is AᵀCA, and its left null space holds the loop currents. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="inclusion-exclusion-principle"></a>**Inclusion–exclusion principle** — P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), which corrects the double counting of outcomes in both events. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="incremental-resistance"></a>**Incremental resistance** — The slope dv/di of a nonlinear element's i–v curve at an operating point, the resistance a small signal sees; for a diode it is about V_T/I. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="indeterminate-form"></a>**Indeterminate form** — An expression such as 0/0, ∞/∞ or ∞ − ∞ whose form alone does not determine a limit; it must be resolved by algebra, standard limits or L'Hôpital's rule. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="indicator-variable"></a>**Indicator variable** — A random variable equal to 1 if an event occurs and 0 otherwise, so its expectation is the event's probability; counts are sums of indicators. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="inductance"></a>**Inductance** — Flux linkage per ampere, L = NΦ/i (henries), so that v = L di/dt; a long solenoid has µ₀N²A/ℓ, a core with reluctance R has N²/R. It scales as turns squared. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="inductive-kick"></a>**Inductive kick** — The large voltage an inductor develops (v = L di/dt) when its current is interrupted abruptly; it can arc switch contacts or break down transistors unless a flyback path is provided. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md). *See also:* [Flyback diode](#flyback-diode).

<a id="initial-value-problem"></a>**Initial-value problem** — A differential equation together with the value of the unknown at a starting time, y(t₀) = y₀, which fixes the arbitrary constant of the general solution. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="initial-value-theorem"></a>**Initial-value theorem** — f(0⁺) = lim sF(s) as s → ∞, valid when F(s) is strictly proper; it checks an inverse transform's starting value without inverting. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Final-value theorem](#final-value-theorem).

<a id="input-bias-current"></a>**Input bias current** — I_B, the small DC current flowing into (or, for PNP input stages, out of) each op-amp input; through a resistance R it produces an error I_B R that is amplified like a signal. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Input offset current](#input-offset-current), [Input offset voltage](#input-offset-voltage).

<a id="input-offset-current"></a>**Input offset current** — I_OS, the difference between an op-amp's two input bias currents; it is the error that remains when the two inputs see equal resistances (a compensation resistor R1∥R2 at the + input). *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Input bias current](#input-bias-current).

<a id="input-offset-voltage"></a>**Input offset voltage** — V_OS, the small DC voltage that, applied between an op-amp's inputs, would bring its output to zero; modeled as a source in series with the + input and amplified by the noise gain (OPA187 10 µV max, LM358 7 mV max at 25 °C). *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Noise gain](#noise-gain), [Input bias current](#input-bias-current).

<a id="instruction-set-architecture-isa"></a>**Instruction-set architecture (ISA)** — The contract between hardware and software, namely the instructions, registers, memory model and exceptions a program can rely on, independent of how a processor implements them. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="instrumentation-amplifier"></a>**Instrumentation amplifier** — A differential amplifier with high input resistance on both inputs and gain set by one resistor, classically two non-inverting stages followed by a difference amplifier, G = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R2/R1); its first stage multiplies the CMRR by its gain. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR)](#common-mode-rejection-ratio-cmrr).

<a id="integer-overflow"></a>**Integer overflow** — A result outside a fixed-width integer type's range; in NumPy arrays and C it wraps around modulo 2^n (uint8 200 + 100 = 44) rather than raising an error. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="integer-promotion"></a>**Integer promotion** — C's rule that integer types narrower than int (char, short, int8_t, uint8_t, int16_t, uint16_t) are converted to int before arithmetic, so uint8_t 200 + 100 is the int 300. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="integral-test"></a>**Integral test** — For a positive decreasing f with a_k = f(k), Σ a_k converges exactly when ∫ f dx does, and the tail after n terms lies between ∫ from n+1 to ∞ and ∫ from n to ∞ of f. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="integrated-device-manufacturer-idm"></a>**Integrated device manufacturer (IDM)** — A chip company that both designs and manufactures its own chips in its own fabs. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="integrating-factor"></a>**Integrating factor** — A multiplier (e^{t/τ} for τ x' + x = u) that turns the left side of a first-order linear ODE into an exact derivative, giving the general solution as an integral of the input. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="integration-by-parts"></a>**Integration by parts** — ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du, the product rule in reverse; used for products such as x e^x, ln x and e^(ax) cos bx. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="integrator"></a>**Integrator** — A circuit or algorithm whose output is the running integral of its input, such as an op-amp with capacitive feedback, v_out = −(1/RC)∫ v_in dt, or a digital accumulator. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md). *See also:* [Integrator (op-amp)](#integrator-op-amp).

<a id="integrator-op-amp"></a>**Integrator (op-amp)** — An op-amp circuit with a capacitor in the feedback path and a resistor at the input, giving v_out = −(1/RC)∫v_in dt; a resistor across the capacitor makes it a "leaky" integrator (a first-order low-pass). *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="interference"></a>**Interference** — The addition of waves arriving with different phases; constructive where path differences are whole wavelengths, destructive at half-wavelengths, redistributing (not destroying) energy. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="interleaving"></a>**Interleaving** — Mixing different problem types within a practice session, which forces choosing the method and improves later performance even though it feels harder during practice. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="intermediate-value-theorem"></a>**Intermediate value theorem** — A continuous function on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b); in particular, a sign change guarantees a root in between. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md). *See also:* [Bisection method](#bisection-method).

<a id="internal-resistance"></a>**Internal resistance** — The series resistance in the model of a real source (an ideal source in series with R_int), which makes the terminal voltage fall as v = V_oc − i R_int under load. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Open-circuit voltage](#open-circuit-voltage), [Short-circuit current](#short-circuit-current).

<a id="interpreter"></a>**Interpreter** — A program that reads source code and executes it at run time (Python compiles it to bytecode first), with no separate build step; mistakes surface only when the offending line runs. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="intrinsic-carrier-concentration"></a>**Intrinsic carrier concentration** — The electron (and equal hole) density of a pure semiconductor, n_i = √(N_c N_v) e^(−E_g/2kT); about 9.65×10⁹ cm⁻³ for silicon at 300 K and rising several hundredfold by 400 K. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="intrinsic-gain"></a>**Intrinsic gain** — g_m·r_o, the largest voltage gain a single transistor can provide, set by its transconductance and output resistance. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md). *See also:* [Transconductance](#transconductance).

<a id="inverse-function"></a>**Inverse function** — The function that undoes a one-to-one function, so that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x; for example ln undoes exp. Solving an equation for a variable applies an inverse. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="inverse-matrix"></a>**Inverse matrix** — A⁻¹ with A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I, existing exactly when det A ≠ 0. Computed by Gauss–Jordan elimination at about 2n³ flops; for solving systems, LU is cheaper and more accurate. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="ir-drop"></a>**IR drop** — The voltage lost along a power-distribution network by current flowing through its resistance, so circuits far from the supply connections see less than the nominal supply voltage. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Electromigration](#electromigration).

<a id="iterative-refinement"></a>**Iterative refinement** — Improving a computed solution of Ax = b by computing the residual r = b − Ax in higher precision, solving A d = r with the existing (often low-precision) factors, and updating x ← x + d; it converges when κ·u_low is well below 1. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="i-v-characteristic"></a>**i–v characteristic** — The plot of all (voltage, current) pairs an element permits; a resistor's is a line through the origin, an ideal voltage source's a vertical line, an ideal current source's a horizontal line. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="letter-j"></a>

## J

<a id="jacobian"></a>**Jacobian** — The determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of a change of variables; its magnitude is the local area or volume scale factor, r for polar and ρ² sin φ for spherical coordinates. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="jensens-inequality"></a>**Jensen's inequality** — For a convex function g, E[g(X)] ≥ g(E[X]); averaging through an exponential or square law raises the result, so leakage or failure rate at the average input underestimates the average. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="jitter"></a>**Jitter** — The deviation of a signal's edges from their ideal times, split into unbounded Gaussian random jitter (RJ) and bounded deterministic jitter (DJ). *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md). *See also:* [Dual-Dirac model](#dual-dirac-model).

<a id="joint-distribution"></a>**Joint distribution** — The joint PMF p(x, y) or PDF f(x, y) of two or more random variables, giving the probability of any combination of values; marginals alone do not determine it. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="jointly-gaussian"></a>**Jointly Gaussian** — Variables whose joint density is the multivariate normal; their marginals and linear combinations are Gaussian, and for them uncorrelated means independent. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="joule-heating"></a>**Joule heating** — The conversion of electrical energy to heat in a resistance, P = I²R = V²/R, or locally p = J · E = ρJ² per unit volume. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="jump-discontinuity"></a>**Jump discontinuity** — A point where both one-sided limits exist but differ, as for the unit step at t = 0 or a capacitor's current at a switching instant. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="junction-voltage-limiting"></a>**Junction voltage limiting** — A Newton-iteration safeguard in SPICE device models that compresses large steps in a pn-junction voltage above a critical voltage to a logarithmic step, preventing the exponential current law from overflowing or stalling convergence. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="jupyter-notebook"></a>**Jupyter notebook** — A document (.ipynb, stored as JSON) of Markdown and code cells whose code runs in a separate kernel process; it saves outputs with the code, so a saved notebook shows results that may not match a fresh run. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md). *See also:* [Hidden state](#hidden-state).

<a id="letter-k"></a>

## K

<a id="kalman-filter"></a>**Kalman filter** — The optimal linear estimator of a state-space system's state from noisy measurements (Kalman, 1960), alternating model-based prediction with measurement correction; widely used in navigation, tracking and sensor fusion. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="kinetic-energy"></a>**Kinetic energy** — The energy of motion, ½mv² for translation and ½Iω² for rotation; by the work–energy theorem, net work equals its change. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="kirchhoffs-current-law-kcl"></a>**Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)** — The algebraic sum of the currents entering a node is zero at every instant; it follows from charge conservation and the lumped assumption that nodes store no charge. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)](#kirchhoffs-voltage-law-kvl), [Lumped-matter discipline](#lumped-matter-discipline).

<a id="kirchhoffs-voltage-law-kvl"></a>**Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)** — The algebraic sum of the voltages around any loop is zero at every instant; it follows from Faraday's law when no changing magnetic flux links the loop outside the elements. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)](#kirchhoffs-current-law-kcl), [Lumped-matter discipline](#lumped-matter-discipline).

<a id="ktc-noise"></a>**kT/C noise** — The thermal noise sampled onto a capacitor through any resistance, with RMS value √(kT/C), about 64 µV for 1 pF at 300 K; independent of the resistance. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="letter-l"></a>

## L

<a id="lhopitals-rule"></a>**L'Hopital's rule** — For 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms, lim f/g = lim f'/g' when the latter exists (named for L'Hôpital); other indeterminate forms are first rewritten as quotients. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="lagrange-multiplier"></a>**Lagrange multiplier** — The factor λ in ∇f = λ∇g at a constrained optimum; it equals the rate of change of the optimal value with the constraint level, a shadow price. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="lagrange-remainder"></a>**Lagrange remainder** — The error of a degree-n Taylor polynomial, f^(n+1)(ξ)(x − a)^(n+1)/(n + 1)! for some ξ between a and x; bounding f^(n+1) bounds the error. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="landauer-limit"></a>**Landauer limit** — The minimum energy to erase one bit of information, kT ln 2 (about 2.9×10^−21 J at 300 K); practical logic uses orders of magnitude more. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="laplace-transform"></a>**Laplace transform** — F(s) = ∫ f(t) e^(−st) dt from 0⁻ to ∞, with s = σ + jω complex; it turns differentiation into multiplication by s (minus initial conditions), so linear constant-coefficient ODEs become algebra. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Transfer function](#transfer-function), [Partial fractions](#partial-fractions).

<a id="law-of-large-numbers"></a>**Law of large numbers** — The sample mean of independent, identically distributed variables converges to their expectation as the sample grows; its standard error falls like σ/√n. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="law-of-total-variance"></a>**Law of total variance** — Var(Y) = E[Var(Y | X)] + Var(E[Y | X]): the average spread within groups plus the spread of the group means. Explains why mixed wafers, lots or tools vary far more than any one group. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="least-significant-bit-lsb"></a>**Least significant bit (LSB)** — The smallest step an N-bit converter resolves, full scale / 2^N; errors and noise are often expressed in LSBs. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="least-squares"></a>**Least squares** — Choosing x̂ to minimize ‖b − Ax‖² when Ax = b has no exact solution; geometrically, Ax̂ is the projection of b onto the column space, so the residual is orthogonal to every column. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md). *See also:* [Normal equations](#normal-equations), [Projection](#projection).

<a id="lenzs-law"></a>**Lenz's law** — The induced current flows so as to oppose the change in flux that produced it (the minus sign in Faraday's law), a consequence of energy conservation. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="level-curve"></a>**Level curve** — The set of points where a function of two variables takes a constant value; a contour line. The gradient is perpendicular to it. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="level-shifter"></a>**Level shifter** — A circuit that translates logic levels between two voltage domains so that families with incompatible thresholds can communicate. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="limit"></a>**Limit** — The value L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a (without equaling a), written lim_{x→a} f(x) = L; the value f(a) itself plays no role. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md). *See also:* [One-sided limit](#one-sided-limit), [Continuity](#continuity).

<a id="limit-comparison-test"></a>**Limit comparison test** — If a_k, b_k > 0 and a_k/b_k tends to a finite positive limit, the series Σ a_k and Σ b_k converge or diverge together. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="line-integral"></a>**Line integral** — The integral of a vector field's component along a path, ∫ F · dr; for a force it is work, for an electric field it is (minus) the voltage difference. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Vector field](#vector-field).

<a id="linear-combination"></a>**Linear combination** — A sum c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k of vectors times scalars. Every matrix–vector product Ax is the linear combination of A's columns with weights x. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="linear-element"></a>**Linear element** — An element whose i–v characteristic is a straight line through the origin (v = Ri); sources, whose lines miss the origin, and diodes are not linear in this sense. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="linear-independence"></a>**Linear independence** — Vectors are independent if the only combination of them equal to 0 has all weights zero; otherwise one of them is a combination of the others. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="linearity"></a>**Linearity** — The property of a system whose response obeys homogeneity and additivity; circuits of resistors, dependent sources, capacitors and inductors are linear, diodes and transistors (beyond small signals) are not. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Homogeneity](#homogeneity), [Superposition](#superposition).

<a id="linearity-of-expectation"></a>**Linearity of expectation** — E[aX + bY + c] = aE[X] + bE[Y] + c for any random variables, independent or not; it gives expected counts as sums of probabilities. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md). *See also:* [Indicator variable](#indicator-variable).

<a id="linearization"></a>**Linearization** — Replacing a function near a point by its tangent line, L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x − a); the error grows as the square of the distance from a. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md). *See also:* [Small-signal model](#small-signal-model).

<a id="link-margin"></a>**Link margin** — Received power minus receiver sensitivity, in dB; the extra loss a radio link can tolerate before it fails. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="linked-list"></a>**Linked list** — A sequence of separately allocated nodes, each pointing to the next; O(1) insertion and removal next to a known node, O(n) search, and poor cache behavior compared with arrays. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="linker"></a>**Linker** — The build stage that combines object files and libraries into one executable, connecting each use of a function or variable to its single definition; a missing definition gives an "undefined reference" error. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="list-comprehension"></a>**List comprehension** — A one-expression loop that builds a list, such as [r \* 1000 for r in values if r > 0]; dict and set comprehensions work the same way. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="load-factor"></a>**Load factor** — For a hash table, entries divided by slots (α = n/m); linear probing needs about ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)) probes per successful search and ½(1 + 1/(1 − α)²) per miss, so tables resize before α reaches about 0.75. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="loading-effect"></a>**Loading effect** — The drop in a source's or divider's output when a load draws current from it; the relative error is about R_source/R_load when the load is much larger. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="loading-factor"></a>**Loading factor** — An ADC's full-scale amplitude divided by the RMS of a noise-like input, k = V_FS/σ; it trades clipping noise (small k) against granular quantization noise (large k). *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="log-log-plot"></a>**Log-log plot** — A graph with both axes logarithmic; a power law y = kxⁿ plots as a straight line of slope n. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="log-normal-distribution"></a>**Log-normal distribution** — The distribution of e^X for Gaussian X; skewed right, with median e^μ and mean e^(μ + σ_ℓ²/2), where σ_ℓ is the standard deviation of X. Subthreshold leakage across devices is approximately log-normal. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="logarithmic-differentiation"></a>**Logarithmic differentiation** — Differentiating ln y instead of y, which turns products, quotients and variable exponents into sums; for example (x^x)' = x^x(1 + ln x). *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="logistic-equation"></a>**Logistic equation** — N' = rN(1 − N/K), growth proportional to the current base and to the remaining room; its S-shaped solution models adoption, epidemics and populations, rising fastest at N = K/2. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="loop"></a>**Loop** — Any closed path through the branches of a circuit that visits no node more than once. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="loop-analysis"></a>**Loop analysis** — The generalization of mesh analysis to any circuit; one loop current per link of a spanning tree (b − n + 1 fundamental loops), with KVL written around each loop. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Spanning tree](#spanning-tree), [Mesh analysis](#mesh-analysis).

<a id="loop-gain"></a>**Loop gain** — The product Aβ of forward gain and feedback fraction around a feedback loop; the closed-loop gain error is about 1/(Aβ). *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="lorentz-force"></a>**Lorentz force** — The total electromagnetic force on a charge, F = q(E + v × B); the magnetic part is perpendicular to the velocity and does no work. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="loss-tangent"></a>**Loss tangent** — tan δ, the ratio of a dielectric's lossy to stored response; it makes waves decay at about πf√ε_r tan δ / c nepers per meter, about 0.025 for FR-4-class laminates and 0.004 for low-loss ones at 10 GHz. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="lot-tolerance-percent-defective-ltpd"></a>**Lot tolerance percent defective (LTPD)** — The defective percentage that a sampling plan rejects with high confidence (usually 90%); zero failures in 230 samples demonstrates LTPD 1. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="low-k-dielectric"></a>**Low-k dielectric** — An interconnect insulator with permittivity below SiO₂'s 3.9 (SiOF, carbon-doped SiOCH at 2.7–3.0, porous films below 2.5, air gaps at 1), used to cut wire capacitance, delay and power. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="low-rank-approximation"></a>**Low-rank approximation** — Keeping the first k terms of the SVD, A_k = Σ_{i≤k} σᵢuᵢvᵢᵀ, the closest rank-k matrix to A (Eckart–Young), with 2-norm error σ_{k+1}. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="lu-factorization"></a>**LU factorization** — A = LU, with L lower triangular holding the elimination multipliers and U upper triangular holding the pivots (PA = LU with row exchanges). Factor once in O(n³), then solve each right-hand side in O(n²). *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="lumped-matter-discipline"></a>**Lumped-matter discipline** — The conditions under which fields can be replaced by voltages and currents in lumped elements obeying KVL and KCL, chiefly that the circuit is small compared with the signal wavelength (or line delay is short compared with edge time). *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md). *See also:* [Transmission line](#transmission-line), [Wavelength](#wavelength).

<a id="letter-m"></a>

## M

<a id="machine-epsilon"></a>**Machine epsilon** — The gap between 1 and the next representable floating-point number, 2^−52 ≈ 2.22×10^−16 for IEEE 754 double precision; the relative precision of a computation. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="magnetic-dipole-moment"></a>**Magnetic dipole moment** — m = NIA for a current loop (A·m²), pointing along the loop's normal; in a field it feels torque m × B and has energy −m · B, and far away it makes a 1/r³ dipole field. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="magnetic-energy-density"></a>**Magnetic energy density** — The energy per unit volume in a magnetic field, u = B²/(2µ) (about 0.4 MJ/m³ at 1 T in air); in a gapped core most of the energy sits in the gap. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="magnetic-field"></a>**Magnetic field** — The field B (tesla; 1 T = 10⁴ gauss) that exerts force qv × B on moving charges; produced by currents and magnetic moments, with field lines that always close on themselves. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="magnetic-flux"></a>**Magnetic flux** — The surface integral of B, Φ = ∬ B · dA, in webers (1 Wb = 1 T·m² = 1 V·s); its rate of change induces EMF. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="magnetic-tunnel-junction"></a>**Magnetic tunnel junction** — Two ferromagnetic layers separated by a nanometer-thin oxide whose tunneling resistance depends on whether their magnetizations are parallel; the storage element of MRAM. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="magnitude"></a>**Magnitude** — The length |z| = √(x² + y²) of a complex number's arrow (also called modulus or absolute value). *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="marginal-distribution"></a>**Marginal distribution** — The distribution of one variable obtained from a joint distribution by summing or integrating out the others. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="markov-chain"></a>**Markov chain** — A random process that moves between states with fixed transition probabilities; its distribution evolves as u_{k+1} = Pu_k, its steady state is the eigenvector for λ = 1, and its convergence rate is set by the second-largest |λ|. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="markovs-inequality"></a>**Markov's inequality** — For a nonnegative random variable, P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="matched-load"></a>**Matched load** — A load equal to the source's Thévenin resistance (for AC, its complex conjugate), which draws the maximum power, at half the open-circuit voltage and 50% efficiency; on a transmission line, a load equal to Z0, which reflects nothing. *First defined in* [06-09](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-09-maximum-power-transfer.md). *See also:* [Maximum power transfer](#maximum-power-transfer), [Conjugate match](#conjugate-match).

<a id="matrix"></a>**Matrix** — A rectangular m×n array of numbers; multiplying it by a vector is a linear map from n-component to m-component vectors. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md). *See also:* [Matrix multiplication](#matrix-multiplication).

<a id="matrix-exponential"></a>**Matrix exponential** — e^{At} = I + At + (At)²/2! + …, the matrix that maps an initial state to the state at time t for x' = Ax; computed by diagonalization, by (sI − A)⁻¹, or numerically by scaling and squaring. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="matrix-multiplication"></a>**Matrix multiplication** — The product AB defined so that (AB)x = A(Bx); entry (i, j) is row i of A dotted with column j of B. It is associative but not commutative, and an n×n product costs n³ multiply–adds. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="maximum-a-posteriori-map-detection"></a>**Maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection** — Choosing the hypothesis with the largest posterior probability given the observation, which minimizes the probability of error; with equal priors it reduces to maximum-likelihood detection. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="maximum-power-point-tracking-mppt"></a>**Maximum power point tracking (MPPT)** — A converter control method that continually adjusts its input operating point (for example by perturb and observe) to extract the most power from a varying source such as a solar cell or thermoelectric generator. *First defined in* [06-09](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-09-maximum-power-transfer.md). *See also:* [Maximum power transfer](#maximum-power-transfer).

<a id="maximum-power-transfer"></a>**Maximum power transfer** — A source of resistance R_s delivers the most power to a load R_L = R_s, namely V_s²/(4R_s), at only 50 % efficiency; used for weak signals (RF, sensors), never for power delivery. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="maxwells-equations"></a>**Maxwell's equations** — Gauss's law, Gauss's law for magnetism, Faraday's law and the Ampère–Maxwell law; with the Lorentz force they are all of classical electromagnetism and predict waves travelling at 1/√(µ₀ε₀) = c. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="mc-dc"></a>**MC/DC** — Modified condition/decision coverage; each condition in a decision is shown to independently change the outcome by a pair of tests differing only in that condition; needs at least N + 1 tests for N conditions; required for DO-178C Level A. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="mean-free-path"></a>**Mean free path** — The average distance a carrier travels between scattering events, λ = v_F τ; about 39–40 nm for electrons in copper at room temperature, which is why narrower copper wires lose conductivity. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="mean-time-between-failures-mtbf"></a>**Mean time between failures (MTBF)** — The reciprocal of a constant failure rate, 1/λ; a fleet statistic (failures per unit-hour), not an expected lifetime of an individual unit. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="mean-time-to-failure-mttf"></a>**Mean time to failure (MTTF)** — The expected lifetime of a non-repairable component, 1/λ for a constant failure rate λ; MTBF is the analogous figure for repairable systems, and the two are often used loosely as synonyms. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md). *See also:* [Mean time between failures (MTBF)](#mean-time-between-failures-mtbf).

<a id="mean-value-theorem"></a>**Mean value theorem** — For f continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside, f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) for some c in (a, b); hence a bound on |f'| bounds the change of f. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="memory-leak"></a>**Memory leak** — Heap memory that is never freed after its last pointer is lost; harmless in a short program, fatal in a long-running device that slowly exhausts its RAM. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="memory-safety"></a>**Memory safety** — The guarantee that a program cannot access memory outside the objects it is entitled to (no overflows, use after free or invalid pointers); C and C++ lack it, Rust, Python and Java provide it, and hardware such as Arm MTE and CHERI can enforce parts of it. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="memory-mapped-i-o"></a>**Memory-mapped I/O** — Accessing hardware peripheral registers at fixed memory addresses with ordinary loads and stores; in C, through volatile pointers to those addresses. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="memoryless-property"></a>**Memoryless property** — P(T > s + t | T > s) = P(T > t), so a surviving item is as good as new; only the exponential (continuous) and geometric (discrete) distributions have it. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="mems"></a>**MEMS** — Micro-electro-mechanical systems, mechanical structures (springs, masses, membranes, resonators) a few micrometers in size made with semiconductor processes and read out electrically; accelerometers, gyroscopes, microphones and timing resonators are MEMS. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="merge-sort"></a>**Merge sort** — Sorting by recursively sorting two halves and merging them in linear time; n log2 n comparisons in every case, stable, needs O(n) extra memory, and within lower-order terms of the comparison-sort lower bound log2(n!). *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="mesh"></a>**Mesh** — In a planar circuit, a loop that encloses no other branch (a window pane of the drawing); the meshes form a set of b − n + 1 independent loops. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="mesh-analysis"></a>**Mesh analysis** — Solving a planar circuit with circulating mesh currents as unknowns, writing KVL around each mesh so that KCL holds automatically; for resistors and voltage sources the result is R·i = v. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Mesh current](#mesh-current), [Nodal analysis](#nodal-analysis), [Supermesh](#supermesh).

<a id="mesh-current"></a>**Mesh current** — A current assigned to circulate around one mesh of a planar circuit; an outer branch carries its mesh current and a shared branch the difference of two. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Mesh](#mesh), [Mesh analysis](#mesh-analysis).

<a id="method-of-undetermined-coefficients"></a>**Method of undetermined coefficients** — Finding a particular solution of a linear ODE by guessing the input's form (constant, polynomial, exponential, sinusoid) with unknown coefficients and matching; multiply the guess by t when it already solves the homogeneous equation. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="miller-effect"></a>**Miller effect** — An impedance connected between the input and output of an inverting amplifier of gain −A looks (1 + A) times smaller (for a capacitance, larger) from the input, because the amplifier multiplies the voltage across it. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Test source](#test-source).

<a id="millmans-theorem"></a>**Millman's theorem** — Practical voltage sources V_k with series resistances R_k in parallel are equivalent to one source of voltage Σ(V_k/R_k)/Σ(1/R_k) with resistance (Σ 1/R_k)^−1. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Source transformation](#source-transformation).

<a id="minimum-energy-point"></a>**Minimum-energy point** — The supply voltage at which a digital circuit's energy per operation is smallest, where falling switching energy balances rising leakage energy; typically a few hundred millivolts in subthreshold CMOS. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="misra-c"></a>**MISRA C** — A widely used set of C coding guidelines for safety-critical embedded software, originating in the automotive industry; the current edition is MISRA C 2025, which targets C11/C18. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="mobility"></a>**Mobility** — Drift speed per unit field, µ = eτ/m (cm²/V·s); copper about 44, lightly doped silicon about 1400 for electrons and 470 for holes. Conductivity is neµ. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="modified-nodal-analysis"></a>**Modified nodal analysis** — The formulation SPICE uses, namely KCL at every node plus extra equations for voltage sources, giving a linear system G·v = i (re-linearized each iteration for nonlinear devices). *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="module-python"></a>**Module (Python)** — A .py file whose functions and names are loaded with import; a package is a folder of modules, and the standard library and pip-installed packages are both used this way. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="moment"></a>**Moment** — E[Xⁿ], the nth moment of a random variable; the first is the mean, and central moments E[(X − μ)ⁿ] give variance (n = 2), skewness (3) and kurtosis (4) after standardizing. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="moment-of-inertia"></a>**Moment of inertia** — Rotational inertia, I = Σ m r² (kg·m²); ½MR² for a uniform disk. It plays the role of mass in rotation. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="moment-generating-function"></a>**Moment-generating function** — M(s) = E[e^{sX}]; for independent variables the MGF of a sum is the product of their MGFs, which turns convolution into multiplication. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="momentum"></a>**Momentum** — The product p = mv (kg·m/s); conserved in an isolated system, and changed only by impulse. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="motional-emf"></a>**Motional EMF** — The EMF Bℓv across a conductor of length ℓ moving at speed v through a field B, the Lorentz force on its charges; the basis of generators. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="multilayer-ceramic-capacitor-mlcc"></a>**Multilayer ceramic capacitor (MLCC)** — A capacitor of many thin ceramic layers interleaved with electrodes; class 1 (C0G) is stable, while class 2 (X5R, X7R) uses BaTiO₃ with ε_r in the thousands and loses capacitance with DC bias and temperature. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="mutable-object"></a>**Mutable object** — An object whose contents can change after creation (Python lists, dicts, sets); immutable objects (numbers, strings, tuples) cannot, which makes sharing them safe. *First defined in* [05-01](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-01-python-fundamentals.md).

<a id="mutual-inductance"></a>**Mutual inductance** — The flux linked in one coil per ampere in another, M (henries), so that v₂ = M di₁/dt; M = k√(L₁L₂). *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="letter-n"></a>

## N

<a id="nan"></a>**NaN** — Not a Number, the IEEE 754 value produced by undefined operations such as 0/0; it propagates through arithmetic and compares unequal to everything, including itself. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="natural-frequency"></a>**Natural frequency** — ω₀ = 1/√(LC) (rad/s), the frequency at which a second-order system would oscillate with no damping; for a mass on a spring, √(k/m). *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="natural-logarithm"></a>**Natural logarithm** — ln y, the inverse of eˣ, defined for y > 0; it turns products into sums, ln(ab) = ln a + ln b. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="natural-response"></a>**Natural response** — The response of a circuit with no sources acting, driven only by the energy initially stored in its capacitors and inductors; for a first-order circuit, an exponential decay. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).
