<a id="negative-feedback"></a>**Negative feedback** — Returning a fraction of a system's output to subtract from its input, which trades excess gain for gains set by passive components, lower sensitivity to the amplifier's parameters and corrected errors. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Loop gain](#loop-gain), [Virtual short](#virtual-short).

<a id="negative-resistance"></a>**Negative resistance** — A port whose current flows out when a positive voltage is applied (v/i < 0), so it delivers power; it requires an active element such as a dependent source with positive feedback, and is the basis of oscillators. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="neper-frequency"></a>**Neper frequency** — α (1/s), the decay rate of a second-order system's envelope e^{−αt}; R/(2L) for a series RLC and 1/(2RC) for a parallel RLC. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="netlist"></a>**Netlist** — A text description of a circuit listing each element, its value and the nodes it connects; the input to a circuit simulator (node 0 is ground). *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="newtons-laws-of-motion"></a>**Newton's laws of motion** — (1) A body with no net force keeps a constant velocity; (2) the net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = dp/dt = ma for constant mass; (3) forces come in equal and opposite pairs. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="newtons-method"></a>**Newton's method** — Root finding by repeatedly solving the tangent-line approximation, x_{k+1} = x_k − f(x_k)/f'(x_k); converges quadratically near a simple root but can diverge from a poor start. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md). *See also:* [Newton–Raphson method](#newton-raphson-method), [Quadratic convergence](#quadratic-convergence).

<a id="newton-raphson-method"></a>**Newton–Raphson method** — An iterative root-finding method, x_{k+1} = x_k − g(x_k)/g′(x_k), that circuit simulators use to solve nonlinear equations; it converges quadratically near a solution but can overshoot far from it. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="nodal-analysis"></a>**Nodal analysis** — Solving a circuit with the voltages of its non-reference nodes as unknowns, writing KCL at each node so that KVL holds automatically; for resistors and current sources the result is G·v = i. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Conductance matrix](#conductance-matrix), [Modified nodal analysis](#modified-nodal-analysis), [Supernode](#supernode).

<a id="node"></a>**Node** — A point where two or more circuit elements connect, together with the ideal wire joining them; in the lumped model it stores no charge. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Branch](#branch), [Loop](#loop).

<a id="node-voltage"></a>**Node voltage** — The voltage of a node relative to the reference node; every branch voltage is the difference of its two node voltages, so node voltages satisfy KVL by construction. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Reference node (ground)](#reference-node-ground), [Nodal analysis](#nodal-analysis).

<a id="noise-figure"></a>**Noise figure** — 10 log₁₀ of the noise factor F, the ratio of a system's total output noise to the part due to a source at 290 K; a receiver's noise floor is −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log₁₀B + NF. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="noise-gain"></a>**Noise gain** — The gain 1 + R2/R1 from a signal at the op-amp's + input (offset voltage, input noise) to its output; it is the same for inverting and non-inverting stages and sets the finite-gain error, about (noise gain)/A. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [Input offset voltage](#input-offset-voltage), [Loop gain](#loop-gain).

<a id="noise-margin"></a>**Noise margin** — The amount of noise a digital connection can tolerate, NM_L = V_IL − V_OL and NM_H = V_OH − V_IH. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="non-recurring-engineering-nre"></a>**Non-recurring engineering (NRE)** — One-time costs of developing a product (design labor, EDA tools, IP licenses, masks, prototypes), as opposed to per-unit manufacturing cost. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="nonlinear-least-squares"></a>**Nonlinear least squares** — Fitting a model whose parameters enter nonlinearly (such as a time constant in an exponential) by iteratively minimizing the sum of squared residuals from a starting guess, as SciPy's curve_fit does; it also estimates the parameters' standard errors. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md). *See also:* [Least squares](#least-squares), [Residual](#residual).

<a id="norm"></a>**Norm** — The length of a vector, ‖v‖ = √(v·v); for a sampled signal, ‖v‖/√N is its RMS value. For complex vectors, ‖v‖² = Σ|vᵢ|². *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md). *See also:* [Dot product](#dot-product).

<a id="normal-equations"></a>**Normal equations** — AᵀA x̂ = Aᵀb, the square system whose solution is the least-squares fit; uniquely solvable when A has independent columns. Software prefers QR or SVD, which avoid squaring the condition number. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="normal-mode"></a>**Normal mode** — A pattern of motion in which every part of a coupled linear system oscillates at the same frequency; mathematically an eigenvector of the system, such as the in-phase and out-of-phase modes of two coupled resonators. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="norton-equivalent"></a>**Norton equivalent** — A current source I_N (the short-circuit current) in parallel with R_th, equivalent at two terminals to any linear network; V_th = R_th I_N. *First defined in* [06-08](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-08-thevenin-and-norton.md). *See also:* [Thevenin equivalent](#thevenin-equivalent), [Short-circuit current](#short-circuit-current).

<a id="null-pointer"></a>**Null pointer** — A pointer value (NULL) that points to no object, used to signal "none" or failure (malloc returns NULL when out of memory); must be checked before dereferencing. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="null-space"></a>**Null space** — N(A), the set of all solutions of Ax = 0; every solution of Ax = b is one particular solution plus a vector in N(A). *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="numerical-aperture"></a>**Numerical aperture** — NA = n sin θ_max, the half-angle of the cone of light a lens or fiber accepts; it sets lithography resolution (∝ 1/NA) and fiber acceptance (√(n₁² − n₂²)). *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="letter-o"></a>

## O

<a id="ohms-law"></a>**Ohm's law** — Current proportional to voltage, V = IR, or locally J = σE; it holds for metals and doped semiconductors at moderate fields and fails at high fields, high frequencies, very short lengths and in junctions. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="one-sided-limit"></a>**One-sided limit** — A limit taken from one side only, x → a⁻ (from below) or x → a⁺ (from above). Circuit analysis writes v(0⁻) and v(0⁺) for the values just before and just after a switching instant. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="open-circuit"></a>**Open circuit** — A break with zero current whatever the voltage across it (R = ∞); an unconnected terminal or an open ideal switch. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Short circuit](#short-circuit).

<a id="open-circuit-voltage"></a>**Open-circuit voltage** — The terminal voltage of a source or network with no load connected (zero current), V_oc. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="operating-point"></a>**Operating point** — The DC voltages and currents of a circuit with its sources at their DC values (capacitors open, inductors shorted); also called the bias point. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="operational-amplifier"></a>**Operational amplifier** — A high-gain differential amplifier, v_out = A(v+ − v−), with very high input resistance and low output resistance, used almost always with negative feedback so that the external components, not A, set the circuit's behavior. *First defined in* [06-10](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-10-ideal-op-amp.md). *See also:* [VCVS](#vcvs), [Virtual short](#virtual-short), [Negative feedback](#negative-feedback).

<a id="optical-fiber"></a>**Optical fiber** — A glass core of slightly higher index than its cladding that guides light by total internal reflection; single-mode fiber (≈ 9 µm core) for long reach, multimode for short links at 850 nm. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="order-of-accuracy"></a>**Order of accuracy** — The exponent p in a numerical method's global error ∝ hᵖ; halving the step divides the error by 2ᵖ (Euler 1, Heun 2, RK4 4). *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="ordinary-differential-equation"></a>**Ordinary differential equation** — An equation relating an unknown function of one variable to its derivatives; its order is that of the highest derivative. A first-order ODE y' = f(t, y) describes any system with a single store of charge, flux, heat or money. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="orthogonal-matrix"></a>**Orthogonal matrix** — A square matrix Q with orthonormal columns, so QᵀQ = I and Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ; it is a rotation or reflection, preserves lengths and angles, and has all singular values equal to 1. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="orthogonality"></a>**Orthogonality** — The property that sinusoids of different integer frequencies multiply to zero average over a common period; it makes Fourier coefficients computable and harmonic powers additive. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="osat"></a>**OSAT** — Outsourced semiconductor assembly and test, a company that packages and tests chips for others. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="output-resistance"></a>**Output resistance** — The Thévenin resistance seen looking into a circuit's output terminals; it sets how much the output voltage sags under load (load regulation) and forms a divider with the next stage's input resistance. *First defined in* [06-08](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-08-thevenin-and-norton.md). *See also:* [Thevenin equivalent](#thevenin-equivalent), [Loading effect](#loading-effect).

<a id="overdamped"></a>**Overdamped** — A second-order system with ζ > 1, whose two real negative roots give a sum of decaying exponentials with no overshoot; more damping makes it slower. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="overkill"></a>**Overkill** — Good parts wrongly rejected by a production test, the false positives of the test. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="overshoot"></a>**Overshoot** — The amount by which a step response exceeds its final value, as a fraction of the step; exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) for a second-order system (16.3% at ζ = 0.5, 4.3% at ζ = 0.707). *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="letter-p"></a>

## P

<a id="p-value"></a>**p-value** — The probability, if the null hypothesis is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="parallel-connection"></a>**Parallel connection** — Elements connected between the same two nodes, so they share the same voltage; parallel conductances add (R1 ∥ R2 = R1R2/(R1 + R2)). *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md). *See also:* [Current divider](#current-divider).

<a id="part-average-testing-pat"></a>**Part Average Testing (PAT)** — An automotive outlier screen (AEC-Q001) that rejects parts passing specification but lying beyond the median ± 6 robust sigma (interquartile range/1.35) of their population. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="partial-derivative"></a>**Partial derivative** — The rate of change of a function of several variables with respect to one of them, all others held fixed, ∂f/∂x; a sensitivity. *First defined in* [01-09](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-09-multivariable-calculus-1.md).

<a id="partial-fractions"></a>**Partial fractions** — Writing a proper rational function as a sum of simple terms, one per factor of the denominator; in circuit analysis each term is a natural mode (pole) of the response. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="partial-pivoting"></a>**Partial pivoting** — Exchanging rows at each elimination step so that the largest-magnitude entry in the column becomes the pivot; it keeps every multiplier at most 1 in magnitude and prevents roundoff from swamping the solution. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="particular-solution"></a>**Particular solution** — Any one solution of a forced (nonhomogeneous) linear ODE; the general solution is a particular solution plus the general homogeneous solution. *First defined in* [02-04](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-04-forced-response-and-resonance.md).

<a id="passive-element"></a>**Passive element** — An element that can never deliver net energy to the rest of a circuit, such as a resistor; sources, which can, are active. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="passive-sign-convention"></a>**Passive sign convention** — Referencing an element's current into the terminal marked +, so that p = vi is the power the element absorbs (negative means it delivers power); SPICE applies it to sources as well. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Electric power](#electric-power).

<a id="peak-to-average-power-ratio-papr"></a>**Peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR)** — Peak power over average power, the square of the crest factor; for noise-like signals such as OFDM it must be quoted at a stated CCDF probability and convention. Instruments use envelope power, in which a constant-envelope carrier is 0 dB and a complex Gaussian is 9.64 dB at 1e-4; for real waveforms a sinusoid is 3.01 dB. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md). *See also:* [Crest factor](#crest-factor), [CCDF](#ccdf).

<a id="performance-power-area-ppa"></a>**Performance, power, area (PPA)** — The three primary metrics traded off in chip design, almost always considered together with cost and schedule. *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="phase"></a>**Phase** — The angle φ in A cos(ωt + φ), fixing where in its cycle a sinusoid is at t = 0. A time delay t_d is a phase lag of ωt_d. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="phase-line"></a>**Phase line** — A one-dimensional picture of an autonomous equation y' = f(y), marking the equilibria and arrows showing where y rises or falls between them. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Equilibrium solution](#equilibrium-solution).

<a id="phase-portrait"></a>**Phase portrait** — The family of trajectories of a two-state system drawn in the state plane; for linear systems it is a node, saddle, spiral or center, set by the trace and determinant of A. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="phased-array"></a>**Phased array** — A row or grid of antennas fed with progressive phase steps so their waves add in a chosen direction, sin θ = Δφ/(kd); steers beams electronically and needs spacing near λ/2 to avoid grating lobes. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="phasor"></a>**Phasor** — The complex number V = V_m∠φ representing the sinusoid V_m cos(ωt + φ) at a known frequency ω, so that v(t) = Re{V e^{jωt}}. This curriculum uses peak-amplitude, cosine-reference phasors. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Sinusoidal steady state](#sinusoidal-steady-state), [Impedance](#impedance).

<a id="phonon"></a>**Phonon** — A quantum of lattice vibration; phonons carry heat, scatter electrons (raising a metal's resistance with temperature) and supply the crystal momentum for light absorption or emission in indirect-gap semiconductors. *First defined in* [04-11](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-11-intro-solid-state-physics.md).

<a id="photoelectric-effect"></a>**Photoelectric effect** — Ejection of electrons from a surface by light, which occurs only if each photon's energy exceeds the work function; the maximum kinetic energy hf − φ grows with frequency, not intensity. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="photon"></a>**Photon** — The quantum of light, a packet of energy E = hf = hc/λ (1239.84 eV·nm divided by the wavelength) and momentum h/λ; light is emitted and absorbed one photon at a time. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="physical-design"></a>**Physical design** — Converting synthesized logic into a manufacturable layout (floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing) and closing timing, power and design-rule signoff. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="pivot"></a>**Pivot** — The diagonal entry used to eliminate the entries below it at each step of Gaussian elimination; it must be nonzero, and should not be small relative to the entries below it. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="planar-circuit"></a>**Planar circuit** — A circuit that can be drawn on a plane with no crossing branches; only planar circuits have meshes. By Kuratowski's theorem a circuit is planar unless it contains a subdivision of K5 or K3,3. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Mesh](#mesh), [Loop analysis](#loop-analysis).

<a id="pointer"></a>**Pointer** — A variable holding a memory address, with a type saying what is stored there (int \*p points to an int); &x gives an address and \*p the object at it. Pointers let functions modify caller data and pass buffers without copying. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md). *See also:* [Dereference](#dereference), [Null pointer](#null-pointer), [Pointer arithmetic](#pointer-arithmetic).

<a id="pointer-arithmetic"></a>**Pointer arithmetic** — Adding an integer to a pointer advances it by whole elements (sizeof the pointed-to type), so a[i] is \*(a + i); subtracting two pointers into one array gives the number of elements between them. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="poisson-distribution"></a>**Poisson distribution** — The count of rare independent events with mean λ: P(k) = e^(−λ) λ^k/k!, the limit of the binomial as n grows with np = λ fixed. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="poisson-process"></a>**Poisson process** — Events occurring independently at a constant average rate; counts in an interval are Poisson and the gaps between events are exponential. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="polar-form"></a>**Polar form** — Writing a complex number by its magnitude and angle, z = r∠θ = r(cos θ + j sin θ) = re^{jθ}. Convenient for multiplication, division, powers and roots. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Rectangular form](#rectangular-form), [Euler's formula](#eulers-formula).

<a id="polarization-dielectric"></a>**Polarization (dielectric)** — The dipole moment per unit volume P (C/m²) induced in a dielectric by electronic, ionic or orientational response; at the dielectric's faces it appears as bound surface charge σ_b = P. *First defined in* [04-04](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-04-potential-capacitance-and-dielectrics.md).

<a id="polarization-light"></a>**Polarization (light)** — The direction in which a transverse wave's electric field oscillates; a polarizer transmits I₀ cos²θ (Malus's law), and reflection at Brewster's angle tan θ_B = n₂/n₁ removes one polarization. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="poles-and-zeros"></a>**Poles and zeros** — The roots of a rational transfer function's denominator (poles) and numerator (zeros). Each pole p gives a natural mode e^(pt), so all poles in the left half-plane means stable; zeros set how much of each mode appears. *First defined in* [02-05](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-05-laplace-transform-for-odes.md). *See also:* [Transfer function](#transfer-function), [Characteristic equation](#characteristic-equation).

<a id="positive-definite-matrix"></a>**Positive definite matrix** — A symmetric matrix with xᵀAx > 0 for every nonzero x; equivalently all eigenvalues positive, or all pivots positive. Grounded conductance matrices, nonsingular covariance matrices and Hessians at strict minima are examples. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="potential-energy"></a>**Potential energy** — Energy stored by position against a conservative force, with F = −dU/dx; mgh for gravity near the Earth and ½k_s x² for a spring. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="power-delivery-network"></a>**Power delivery network** — The regulators, board and package wiring, and decoupling capacitors that carry current from the supply to the transistors; its inductance and the die's capacitance form a resonant tank that causes supply droop on load steps. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="power-factor"></a>**Power factor** — Real power divided by apparent power; cos φ for sinusoids with phase difference φ, and lower still when the current is distorted. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="power-law"></a>**Power law** — A relation y = kxⁿ; doubling x multiplies y by 2ⁿ, and on log-log axes it is a straight line with slope n. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md). *See also:* [Log-log plot](#log-log-plot).

<a id="power-over-ethernet-poe"></a>**Power over Ethernet (PoE)** — Delivering DC power over Ethernet cabling (IEEE 802.3af, at and bt) at up to 57 V; the device receives the source's class power minus the cable's I²R loss (90 W at the source gives 71.3 W at the device for Type 4). *First defined in* [06-08](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-08-thevenin-and-norton.md). *See also:* [Thevenin equivalent](#thevenin-equivalent).

<a id="power-rating"></a>**Power rating** — The power a component can dissipate continuously at a stated ambient temperature, derated above it; designers usually run parts well below it. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="power-rule"></a>**Power rule** — d/dx xⁿ = n xⁿ⁻¹, valid for every real exponent n (for x > 0). *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="power-series"></a>**Power series** — Σ c_k (x − a)^k; it converges inside a radius of convergence, where it can be differentiated and integrated term by term. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="power-spectral-density"></a>**Power spectral density** — The distribution of a stationary process's average power over frequency, in power per hertz; the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation. Circuit noise densities are usually one-sided. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="poynting-vector"></a>**Poynting vector** — S = E × B/µ₀ (W/m²), the power flow per unit area in an electromagnetic field; it shows energy entering resistors and capacitors through the surrounding fields, and gives a plane wave's intensity E₀²/(2η₀). *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="ppk"></a>**Ppk** — The process performance index, Cpk's formula with the overall standard deviation of all the data (including drift and lot-to-lot shifts) instead of the within-subgroup σ; equal to Cpk only for a process in statistical control. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="preprocessor"></a>**Preprocessor** — The first stage of a C build, which rewrites source text according to lines starting with *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="principal-component-analysis"></a>**Principal component analysis** — Finding the eigenvectors of a data set's covariance matrix (equivalently the singular vectors of the centered data), ordered by the variance they carry, to describe or compress the data with a few uncorrelated components. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="probability-density-function"></a>**Probability density function** — A non-negative function f(x) with total area 1, whose area over an interval is the probability of landing in it; the density itself is not a probability and can exceed 1. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="probability-mass-function-pmf"></a>**Probability mass function (PMF)** — For a discrete random variable, p_X(k) = P(X = k); the values are non-negative and sum to 1. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="process-capability-cp-cpk"></a>**Process capability (Cp, Cpk)** — Cp = (USL − LSL)/(6σ) compares the specification window with the process spread; Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/(3σ) also charges for an off-center mean. Automotive defaults (AIAG, 1995 manuals): Cpk ≥ 1.33 for stable ongoing production; preliminary studies and significant characteristics are judged on Ppk, expecting ≥ 1.67. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="process-design-kit-pdk"></a>**Process design kit (PDK)** — The files a foundry gives designers to use its process, including device models, design rules, layer definitions and often standard-cell libraries, abstracting the fab's recipes. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="product-rule"></a>**Product rule** — (fg)' = f'g + fg'; the derivative of a product has one term for each factor's change. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="projection"></a>**Projection** — The closest point to b on the line through a, p = (a·b / a·a) a, characterized by the error b − p being perpendicular to a; the basis of least squares. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="proof-mass"></a>**Proof mass** — The suspended mass in an accelerometer or gyroscope whose displacement relative to its package measures acceleration (deflection a/ω₀² below resonance) or rotation. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md).

<a id="propagation-delay"></a>**Propagation delay** — The time from an input transition to the output crossing 50 % of its swing; for an RC model, τ·ln 2 ≈ 0.69τ. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="letter-q"></a>

## Q

<a id="q-format"></a>**Q format** — Notation Qm.f for fixed-point numbers with m integer and f fractional bits; Q15 is a 16-bit signed fraction in [−1, 1 − 2^−15] with resolution 3.05×10^−5. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="q-function"></a>**Q-function** — Q(x), the probability that a standard normal random variable exceeds x; it gives error probabilities for decisions in Gaussian noise and falls off extremely fast (Q(6) ≈ 1e-9). *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="quadratic-convergence"></a>**Quadratic convergence** — Convergence in which each error is proportional to the square of the previous one, so the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="quality-factor"></a>**Quality factor** — Q = 1/(2ζ) = ω₀ × energy stored / power dissipated; the amplitude decays by a factor e in Q/π cycles, and Q also sets the sharpness of resonance. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Damping ratio](#damping-ratio).

<a id="quantization-noise"></a>**Quantization noise** — The rounding error of an ADC, modeled as uniform over ±½ LSB, with RMS Δ/√12 ≈ 0.29 LSB; it sets the ideal SNR of 6.02N + 1.76 dB. *First defined in* [01-07](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-07-applications-of-integration.md).

<a id="quantum-confinement"></a>**Quantum confinement** — The rise and spreading of energy levels when a particle is squeezed into a region comparable to its de Broglie wavelength, E_n = n²h²/(8mL²) for an infinite well; it tunes quantum-well lasers and quantum-dot colors. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="quantum-tunneling"></a>**Quantum tunneling** — Passage of a particle through a barrier higher than its energy, with probability falling roughly as e^(−2κd), κ = √(2m(V₀ − E))/ħ; it causes gate-oxide leakage and enables flash memory, STM and tunnel diodes. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="qubit"></a>**Qubit** — A two-level quantum system in a superposition α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ with |α|² + |β|² = 1; measurement returns 0 or 1 with probabilities |α|² and |β|², and n qubits need 2ⁿ amplitudes to describe classically. *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="queue"></a>**Queue** — A first-in-first-out collection with enqueue at the back and dequeue at the front, O(1) each; implemented with a ring buffer or a linked list. A priority queue instead removes the smallest key first. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="quotient-rule"></a>**Quotient rule** — (f/g)' = (f'g − fg')/g², valid where g ≠ 0. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="letter-r"></a>

## R

<a id="radian"></a>**Radian** — The angle that subtends an arc equal to the radius; 2π rad = 360° and 1 rad ≈ 57.30°. Calculus formulas for sin and cos hold only in radians. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="radius-of-convergence"></a>**Radius of convergence** — The distance from a power series' center within which it converges; it equals the distance to the nearest singularity, including complex ones. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="random-process"></a>**Random process** — A rule assigning a waveform to each outcome of an experiment; at any fixed time its value is a random variable, and the collection of waveforms is the ensemble. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="random-seed"></a>**Random seed** — The starting value of a pseudo-random generator (np.random.default_rng(seed)); the same seed reproduces the same numbers, making simulations and tests repeatable. *First defined in* [05-02](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-02-numpy-and-vectorization.md).

<a id="random-variable"></a>**Random variable** — A function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment, such as the number of bit errors in a packet or the noise voltage at a sampling instant. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="random-walk"></a>**Random walk** — The running sum (integral) of white noise, whose spread grows as √t without bound; it models accumulated phase error in free-running oscillators. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="rank"></a>**Rank** — The number of pivots of a matrix, equal to the dimension of its column space (and of its row space). Numerically, the rank counts singular values above a stated tolerance. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md). *See also:* [Column space](#column-space), [Null space](#null-space), [Rank–nullity theorem](#rank-nullity-theorem).

<a id="rank-nullity-theorem"></a>**Rank–nullity theorem** — For an m×n matrix of rank r, dim C(A) + dim N(A) = r + (n − r) = n. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="ratio-test"></a>**Ratio test** — A series converges if |a_{k+1}/a_k| tends to a limit below 1 and diverges if above 1; suited to factorials and powers. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="rayleigh-criterion"></a>**Rayleigh criterion** — Two point sources are just resolved when one's diffraction peak falls on the other's first dark ring, 1.22λ/D apart in angle; in lithography the analogous limit is CD = k₁λ/NA with k₁ ≥ 0.25. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="rayleigh-distribution"></a>**Rayleigh distribution** — The distribution of the envelope R of a complex Gaussian signal, f(r) = (2r/P̄)e^(−r²/P̄), when the power R² is exponential with mean P̄; mean √(πP̄)/2. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="reactance"></a>**Reactance** — The imaginary part X of an impedance Z = R + jX, in ohms. Positive for inductors (ωL), negative for capacitors (−1/(ωC)). *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="reciprocity"></a>**Reciprocity** — In a linear network of resistors (and other reciprocal elements), the response at node k to a current injected at node j equals the response at j to the same current injected at k; mathematically, the resistance matrix G⁻¹ is symmetric. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="rectangular-form"></a>**Rectangular form** — Writing a complex number by its components, z = x + jy. Convenient for addition and subtraction. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md). *See also:* [Polar form](#polar-form).

<a id="reduction-of-order"></a>**Reduction of order** — Finding a second solution of a linear ODE by writing y = u(t)y₁(t) with a known solution y₁; for a repeated characteristic root it gives te^{−αt}. *First defined in* [02-03](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-03-second-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="reed-solomon-code"></a>**Reed–Solomon code** — A block code over m-bit symbols; RS(n, k) sends n symbols with k data symbols and corrects up to t = (n − k)/2 wrong symbols per codeword, as in Ethernet's RS(544,514). *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="reference-direction"></a>**Reference direction** — The arrow (for current) or the + and − marks (for voltage) chosen before solving a circuit; a negative result means the actual direction or polarity is opposite to the reference. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md).

<a id="reference-node-ground"></a>**Reference node (ground)** — The node chosen as zero volts, relative to which every other node voltage is quoted; a bookkeeping choice that need not be connected to the earth. *First defined in* [06-01](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-01-charge-current-voltage-power.md). *See also:* [Voltage](#voltage), [Grounding](#grounding).

<a id="reflection-coefficient"></a>**Reflection coefficient** — Γ = (R − Z0)/(R + Z0), the ratio of reflected to incident wave voltage at a termination R on a line of characteristic impedance Z0; +1 for an open, −1 for a short, 0 for a matched load. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="regeneration"></a>**Regeneration** — Restoring a signal to clean logic levels at each stage, so that noise does not accumulate along a chain; the key advantage of digital over analog processing. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="regression-line"></a>**Regression line** — The conditional mean E[Y | X = x] = μ_Y + ρ(σ_Y/σ_X)(x − μ_X) of jointly Gaussian variables, the best prediction of Y from X; the remaining spread is σ_Y√(1 − ρ²). *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="regression-test"></a>**Regression test** — A test kept permanently in a suite to make sure a fixed bug or a verified behavior does not silently return; in chip design, the nightly regression is the whole suite of such tests. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="related-rates"></a>**Related rates** — Rates of change linked by differentiating a relationship among quantities with respect to time, for example i = V dC/dt for a moving-plate capacitor. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="relative-permeability"></a>**Relative permeability** — The factor µ_r in B = µ_r µ₀ H for a linear magnetic material; near 1 for most materials, hundreds to tens of thousands for ferromagnets below saturation. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="relative-permittivity"></a>**Relative permittivity** — The factor ε_r by which a material's polarization reduces the field of a given free charge, so that ε = ε_r ε₀; about 11.7 for silicon and 3.9 for thermal SiO₂. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="reluctance"></a>**Reluctance** — The magnetic-circuit analogue of resistance, R = l/(µ_r µ₀ A) (A/Wb); flux = NI/R, series reluctances add, and a small air gap often dominates a core's reluctance. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="removable-discontinuity"></a>**Removable discontinuity** — A point where a function's limit exists but its value is missing or different; redefining the value as the limit removes it (for example sin x/x at 0). *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="repeater"></a>**Repeater** — A buffer inserted along a long on-chip wire to break it into shorter segments, converting delay that grows with the square of length into delay that grows linearly. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="reproducibility"></a>**Reproducibility** — The property that someone else can regenerate a result from the recorded code, data and environment and get the same numbers; achieved by scripting every step, pinning versions, seeding randomness and fingerprinting data. *First defined in* [05-04](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-04-reproducible-workflows.md).

<a id="requirement"></a>**Requirement** — A statement of what a system must do (functional) or how well (non-functional, e.g. power, latency, reliability); good requirements are specific, measurable, testable, unambiguous and free of design. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md). *See also:* [Traceability](#traceability).

<a id="residual"></a>**Residual** — The difference between a measured value and a model's prediction (or, in root-finding, the value f(x) at a claimed root); random residuals at the noise level mean the model is adequate, while a systematic pattern means physics is missing. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md).

<a id="resistance"></a>**Resistance** — The ratio of voltage to current for a resistor, R = v/i, in ohms (V/A); for a uniform conductor R = ρL/A. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Conductance](#conductance), [Ohm's law](#ohms-law).

<a id="resistivity"></a>**Resistivity** — The material property ρ = 1/σ (Ω·m) that sets resistance R = ρL/A; copper is 1.68 µΩ·cm in bulk and rises with temperature and in wires narrower than its mean free path. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="resonance"></a>**Resonance** — The condition in an LC-containing circuit where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel (ω₀ = 1/√(LC) in a series RLC), making the impedance purely resistive and the response peak. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="respin"></a>**Respin** — A new manufacturing pass of a chip with corrected masks after a bug or shortfall is found in silicon, either metal-only or full-layer. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="responsivity"></a>**Responsivity** — A photodetector's output current per unit optical power, R = ηeλ/(hc) = ηλ[µm]/1.24 A/W, where η is the quantum efficiency (electrons per incident photon). *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="reticle-limit"></a>**Reticle limit** — The largest area one lithography exposure can print, 26 mm × 33 mm ≈ 858 mm² on standard scanners (half that with High-NA EUV); it caps the size of a single die without stitching. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md). *See also:* [Chiplet](#chiplet).

<a id="retrieval-practice"></a>**Retrieval practice** — Learning by actively recalling information (self-testing, solving problems) rather than re-reading it; the "testing effect" is among the most robust findings in learning science. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="riemann-sum"></a>**Riemann sum** — An approximation of accumulated quantity, Σ f(x_k\*) Δx, from samples of f on a partition; left, right, midpoint and trapezoid are common choices. *First defined in* [01-05](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-05-integrals.md). *See also:* [Definite integral](#definite-integral).

<a id="ring-buffer"></a>**Ring buffer** — A fixed-size array used as a FIFO queue whose read and write positions wrap around; with free-running unsigned counters and a power-of-two size, the count is head − tail and the slot is counter AND (size − 1). Standard between interrupts and main loops. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="rise-time"></a>**Rise time** — The time a response takes to go from 10 % to 90 % of its total change; τ·ln 9 ≈ 2.2τ for a single pole, so t_r ≈ 0.35/f_3dB. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="rms-value"></a>**RMS value** — Root-mean-square value, √(average of v²). For a sinusoid of amplitude V_m it is V_m/√2; it is the value that delivers the same average power to a resistor as a DC voltage of that size. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="root-sum-of-squares-rss"></a>**Root sum of squares (RSS)** — Combining independent error contributions as the square root of the sum of their squares; less pessimistic than adding them worst-case. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="root-finding"></a>**Root-finding** — Solving f(x) = 0 numerically, the way a nonlinear circuit (a diode with a resistor) is solved; bracketing methods need an interval where f changes sign, while guess-based methods need a good starting point and can fail silently. *First defined in* [05-03](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-03-scipy-sympy-matplotlib.md). *See also:* [Bisection method](#bisection-method), [Brent's method](#brents-method), [Newton's method](#newtons-method).

<a id="root-sum-square-rss"></a>**Root-sum-square (RSS)** — Combining independent random contributions as the square root of the sum of their squares, because their variances add; it gives a total at a stated confidence level only if each input is given at that same level. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Error budget](#error-budget), [Worst-case analysis](#worst-case-analysis).

<a id="roots-of-unity"></a>**Roots of unity** — The N complex numbers e^{j2πk/N} (k = 0 … N−1) whose N-th power is 1, equally spaced on the unit circle. They are the twiddle factors of the FFT. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="rtl"></a>**RTL** — Register-transfer level, the description of digital logic in an HDL (Verilog/SystemVerilog) as registers and the logic between them, from which synthesis produces gates. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="rule-of-three"></a>**Rule of three** — With zero failures in n independent trials, the 95% upper confidence bound on the failure probability is about 3/n. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="runge-kutta-method"></a>**Runge–Kutta method** — An explicit one-step ODE integrator that combines several slope evaluations within each step; the classical RK4 method uses four and is fourth-order accurate. *First defined in* [02-10](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-10-numerical-methods.md).

<a id="r-2r-ladder"></a>**R–2R ladder** — A resistor network of series R and shunt 2R sections in which each node sees R looking onward, so currents halve at every rung; the basis of many digital-to-analog converters. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="letter-s"></a>

## S

<a id="saddle-point"></a>**Saddle point** — An equilibrium whose matrix has real eigenvalues of opposite sign (negative determinant); trajectories approach along one eigenvector and leave along the other, so it is unstable. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md).

<a id="sample-function"></a>**Sample function** — One waveform of a random process, such as the noise recorded from one particular amplifier. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="sample-space"></a>**Sample space** — The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, such as every possible error pattern in a block of bits; events are subsets of it. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="sample-variance"></a>**Sample variance** — S² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/(n − 1), unbiased for σ² because one degree of freedom is used up estimating the mean. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="sample-and-hold"></a>**Sample-and-hold** — A circuit that connects a capacitor to a signal through a switch (sample), then disconnects it to hold the voltage while it is converted; its settling and kT/C noise limit ADC accuracy. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="sanitizer"></a>**Sanitizer** — Compiler-inserted run-time checks (UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, AddressSanitizer) that report undefined behavior and memory errors with the source line; used in testing, at roughly 2x run-time cost. *First defined in* [05-05](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-05-c-fundamentals.md).

<a id="saturation-arithmetic"></a>**Saturation arithmetic** — Arithmetic that clamps results to the largest or smallest representable value instead of wrapping around, so an overflowing signal clips rather than jumping to the opposite extreme. *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="saturation-flux-density"></a>**Saturation flux density** — The flux density B_s at which a ferromagnetic core is fully magnetized; beyond it the core adds nothing and inductance collapses. About 0.49 T for N87 ferrite at 25 °C (0.39 T at 100 °C), 1.5–1.8 T for silicon steel. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="schrodinger-equation"></a>**Schrodinger equation** — The wave equation of quantum mechanics, −(ħ²/2m)ψ″ + Vψ = Eψ in its time-independent 1-D form; its allowed solutions give the energy levels of wells, atoms and crystals. (Written Schrödinger in the text.) *First defined in* [04-10](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-10-intro-quantum-mechanics.md).

<a id="second-derivative"></a>**Second derivative** — The derivative of the derivative, f''(x) or d²y/dx²; it measures curvature (concavity) and, for position, acceleration. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="second-derivative-test"></a>**Second derivative test** — At a critical point, f'' < 0 indicates a local maximum and f'' > 0 a local minimum; f'' = 0 is inconclusive. The size of f'' measures how sharp the optimum is. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="self-checking-testbench"></a>**Self-checking testbench** — A testbench that compares the design's outputs with independently computed expected values and reports pass or fail automatically, rather than relying on a human reading waveforms. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md).

<a id="self-resonant-frequency"></a>**Self-resonant frequency** — The frequency at which an inductor's winding capacitance resonates with its inductance; above it the part behaves as a capacitor, not an inductor. *First defined in* [04-07](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-07-faraday-lenz-and-inductance.md).

<a id="semantic-versioning"></a>**Semantic versioning** — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers where MAJOR signals incompatible changes, MINOR compatible new features and PATCH compatible fixes. *First defined in* [05-09](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-09-software-engineering-practices.md).

<a id="semilog-plot"></a>**Semilog plot** — A graph with one logarithmic axis (usually the vertical); an exponential function plots as a straight line on it. *First defined in* [01-01](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-01-functions-models-and-units.md).

<a id="separable-equation"></a>**Separable equation** — A first-order equation y' = a(t)b(y), solved by integrating dy/b(y) = a(t) dt; constant solutions where b(y) = 0 must be checked separately. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md).

<a id="sequence"></a>**Sequence** — An ordered list a₁, a₂, a₃, …; it converges to L if its terms approach L as n grows. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="series"></a>**Series** — An infinite sum Σ a_k, defined as the limit of its partial sums; it converges if that limit is finite. *First defined in* [01-08](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-08-sequences-series-and-taylor.md).

<a id="series-connection"></a>**Series connection** — Elements joined end to end with nothing else connected at the nodes between them, so they carry the same current; series resistances add. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md). *See also:* [Voltage divider](#voltage-divider).

<a id="settling-time"></a>**Settling time** — The time a response takes to come and stay within a specified error band of its final value; τ·ln(1/ε) for a first-order system, and (N+1)·ln 2 · τ to reach ½ LSB of an N-bit converter. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="shannon-capacity"></a>**Shannon capacity** — The maximum error-free data rate of a channel with bandwidth B and signal-to-noise ratio SNR, C = B log2(1 + SNR). *First defined in* [00-01](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-01-map-of-electrical-engineering.md).

<a id="sheet-resistance"></a>**Sheet resistance** — The resistance of a square of a thin film, R_s = ρ/t (Ω/□); a trace's resistance is R_s times its number of squares, L/W. *First defined in* [04-05](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-05-current-resistance-and-conduction.md).

<a id="short-circuit"></a>**Short circuit** — An element or connection with zero voltage across it whatever its current (R = 0); an ideal wire or a closed ideal switch. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md). *See also:* [Open circuit](#open-circuit).

<a id="short-circuit-current"></a>**Short-circuit current** — The current a source or network would deliver into a short circuit, I_sc = V_oc/R_int for a linear model; a model parameter, not a safe operating point. *First defined in* [06-02](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-02-circuit-elements-and-ohms-law.md).

<a id="shot-noise"></a>**Shot noise** — Noise from the random, independent arrival of discrete charges across a barrier, with one-sided density 2qI; it follows from Poisson statistics. *First defined in* [03-06](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-06-random-processes-preview.md).

<a id="si-base-units"></a>**SI base units** — The seven base units of the International System of Units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol, cd), from which all others, including V, Ω, F and H, are derived. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="side-channel"></a>**Side channel** — An unintended leak of information through physical behavior such as timing, power consumption or electromagnetic emission, which can reveal secrets that the logical abstraction hides. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md).

<a id="sign-extension"></a>**Sign extension** — Widening a two's-complement value by copying its sign bit into the new high bits (8-bit 0xFB, −5, becomes 16-bit 0xFFFB); needed by hand for odd-width fields such as 12-bit sensor readings, e.g. (x XOR 2^(k−1)) − 2^(k−1). *First defined in* [05-07](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-07-bit-manipulation.md).

<a id="simple-harmonic-oscillator"></a>**Simple harmonic oscillator** — A system whose restoring force is proportional to displacement, m ẍ = −k_s x, which oscillates sinusoidally at ω₀ = √(k_s/m) while energy sloshes between kinetic and potential stores. *First defined in* [04-01](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-01-mechanics-essentials.md). *See also:* [Quality factor](#quality-factor), [Force–voltage analogy](#force-voltage-analogy).

<a id="simpsons-rule"></a>**Simpson's rule** — Numerical integration fitting parabolas through triples of samples, with weights h/3 × (1, 4, 2, 4, …, 4, 1); its error falls as h⁴. *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="sinc-function"></a>**Sinc function** — sin(x)/x (sometimes normalized as sin(πx)/(πx)); its removable discontinuity at 0 is filled with the limit 1. It appears throughout sampling and Fourier analysis. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="singular-matrix"></a>**Singular matrix** — A square matrix whose columns are dependent, so Ax = b has no solution for most b and infinitely many for the rest; elimination on it cannot produce a full set of nonzero pivots. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="singular-value-decomposition"></a>**Singular value decomposition** — A = UΣVᵀ for any matrix, with orthogonal U and V and non-negative singular values on the diagonal of Σ; it maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid with semi-axes σᵢ. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md). *See also:* [Low-rank approximation](#low-rank-approximation), [Condition number](#condition-number).

<a id="sinusoid"></a>**Sinusoid** — A signal of the form A cos(ωt + φ), with amplitude A, angular frequency ω and phase φ. This curriculum always uses the cosine as the reference form. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="sinusoidal-steady-state"></a>**Sinusoidal steady state** — The response of a stable linear system to a sinusoidal input after transients have died out, a sinusoid at the input frequency whose amplitude and phase follow from phasor analysis. *First defined in* [02-01](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-01-complex-numbers-euler-and-phasors.md).

<a id="skin-effect"></a>**Skin effect** — The crowding of AC current toward a conductor's surface, within a skin depth δ = √(ρ/(πfμ)) (about 0.21 mm in copper at 100 kHz), which raises resistance at high frequency. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md).

<a id="slew-rate"></a>**Slew rate** — The maximum rate of change dv/dt an amplifier's output can produce, usually in V/µs; it limits the full-power bandwidth to SR/(2πV_p). *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="small-signal-conductance"></a>**Small-signal conductance** — The slope dI/dV of a nonlinear device's I–V curve at its operating point; for a diode g_d ≈ I/V_T, so r_d = V_T/I ≈ 26 Ω at 1 mA. *First defined in* [01-03](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-03-derivatives.md).

<a id="small-signal-model"></a>**Small-signal model** — A linear model of a nonlinear device valid for small deviations about a DC operating point, built from slopes such as g_d = dI/dV or a transistor's g_m. *First defined in* [01-04](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-04-applications-of-derivatives.md).

<a id="snells-law"></a>**Snell's law** — n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ for refraction at a boundary (angles from the normal), from requiring wavefronts to match along the surface. *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="soft-error"></a>**Soft error** — A non-destructive change of a stored bit caused by a particle strike (neutrons or alpha particles); it is corrected by rewriting, and its rate is quoted in FIT per megabit. *First defined in* [03-02](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-02-random-variables-and-distributions.md).

<a id="solenoid"></a>**Solenoid** — A long helical coil whose interior field is nearly uniform, B = µ₀nI with n turns per meter, and whose exterior field is small. *First defined in* [04-06](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-06-magnetic-fields-and-forces.md).

<a id="solid-angle"></a>**Solid angle** — The 3-D analogue of an angle, Ω = A/r², the area a cone cuts from a sphere over the radius squared, in steradians; a full sphere is 4π sr. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).

<a id="source-degeneration"></a>**Source degeneration** — A resistor R_S in a transistor's source (or R_E in a bipolar emitter) that feeds back a voltage opposing the input, cutting the gain to about −R_D/(R_S + 1/g_m) but making it set by resistors rather than by the device. *First defined in* [06-06](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-06-dependent-sources.md). *See also:* [Transconductance](#transconductance).

<a id="source-transformation"></a>**Source transformation** — Replacing a voltage source V_s in series with R by a current source V_s/R in parallel with R, or the reverse; the two are equivalent at their terminals but not internally. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Millman's theorem](#millmans-theorem).

<a id="spaced-repetition"></a>**Spaced repetition** — A review method, often implemented in flashcard software such as Anki, that schedules each item at expanding intervals just before it would be forgotten. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md).

<a id="spacing-effect"></a>**Spacing effect** — The finding that practice distributed over time produces more durable learning than the same practice massed together; the best gap grows with how long the material must be retained. *First defined in* [00-03](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-03-how-to-study-this-curriculum.md). *See also:* [Spaced repetition](#spaced-repetition).

<a id="spanning-tree"></a>**Spanning tree** — A set of n − 1 branches that connects all n nodes of a circuit without forming a loop; each remaining branch (a link) closes one independent loop, giving b − n + 1 independent KVL equations. *First defined in* [06-03](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-03-kirchhoffs-laws.md).

<a id="sparse-matrix"></a>**Sparse matrix** — A matrix whose entries are almost all zero, stored and factored by keeping only the nonzeros; circuit and power-grid matrices have a few nonzeros per row. *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="specific-absorption-rate-sar"></a>**Specific absorption rate (SAR)** — RF power absorbed per kilogram of tissue (W/kg); exposure limits include 1.6 W/kg averaged over 1 g (US FCC) and 2 W/kg over 10 g (ICNIRP), so limits must be compared with their averaging mass. *First defined in* [04-08](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-08-maxwell-preview.md).

<a id="spectral-theorem"></a>**Spectral theorem** — Every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, A = QΛQᵀ = Σ λᵢqᵢqᵢᵀ. *First defined in* [02-08](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-08-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors.md).

<a id="spice"></a>**SPICE** — Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis, the standard family of circuit simulators that solve a netlist's nodal equations for DC, AC and transient behavior; ngspice is an open-source version. *First defined in* [00-04](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-04-toolchain-walkthrough.md). *See also:* [Netlist](#netlist), [Modified nodal analysis](#modified-nodal-analysis).

<a id="squeeze-theorem"></a>**Squeeze theorem** — If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and g and h share the limit L, then f also tends to L. Used to prove sin θ/θ → 1. *First defined in* [01-02](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-02-limits-and-continuity.md).

<a id="stack-data-structure"></a>**Stack (data structure)** — A last-in-first-out collection with push and pop at one end, O(1) each; used for function calls, undo histories, expression evaluation and bracket matching. *First defined in* [05-08](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-08-data-structures-and-algorithms.md).

<a id="stack-memory"></a>**Stack (memory)** — The region holding local variables and function call frames, allocated on function entry and released on return; fast but small (megabytes on desktops, kilobytes on MCUs), and a pointer to a returned function's local dangles. *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="stamp"></a>**Stamp** — The fixed pattern of matrix entries one circuit element contributes to the nodal or MNA equations; a resistor of conductance g between nodes a and b adds +g at (a, a) and (b, b) and −g at (a, b) and (b, a). *First defined in* [02-06](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-06-vectors-matrices-and-linear-systems.md).

<a id="standard-deviation"></a>**Standard deviation** — The square root of the variance, σ, in the units of the random variable; for a signal it is the AC RMS value. *First defined in* [03-03](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-03-expectation-and-functions-of-rvs.md).

<a id="standard-error"></a>**Standard error** — The standard deviation of an estimate; for the mean of n independent samples, σ/√n. *First defined in* [03-04](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-04-joint-distributions-and-clt.md).

<a id="standing-wave"></a>**Standing wave** — The sum of equal waves travelling in opposite directions, 2A cos(kx) cos(ωt), with fixed nodes half a wavelength apart; confined between reflectors it sets resonant modes such as f_n = nv/(2L). *First defined in* [04-09](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-09-waves-and-optics.md).

<a id="star-ground"></a>**Star ground** — A grounding layout in which each circuit has its own return conductor to a single common point at the supply, so that no return impedance is shared between noisy and sensitive circuits. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Common-impedance coupling](#common-impedance-coupling).

<a id="state-variable"></a>**State variable** — A variable that fully captures a circuit's stored energy and memory, namely capacitor voltages and inductor currents. Knowing them at one instant (plus the inputs) determines the future response. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="state-space-model"></a>**State-space model** — The description x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du of a linear system, with state vector x (for circuits, capacitor voltages and inductor currents); the eigenvalues of A are the system's poles. *First defined in* [02-09](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-09-systems-of-odes-and-matrix-exponential.md). *See also:* [State variable](#state-variable), [Matrix exponential](#matrix-exponential), [Transfer function](#transfer-function).

<a id="static-discipline"></a>**Static discipline** — The rule defining valid digital levels with separate output (V_OL, V_OH) and input (V_IL, V_IH) thresholds, so that every gate restores clean levels and leaves noise margins. *First defined in* [00-02](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-02-the-abstraction-stack.md). *See also:* [Noise margin](#noise-margin).

<a id="statistical-independence"></a>**Statistical independence** — Events A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B), so learning one tells nothing about the other; several events are independent only if every subcollection satisfies the product rule. *First defined in* [03-01](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-01-probability-in-ee-language.md).

<a id="statistical-power"></a>**Statistical power** — The probability that a test rejects the null hypothesis when a specified alternative is true, 1 − β; it grows with sample size and effect size. *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="statistical-process-control-spc"></a>**Statistical process control (SPC)** — Monitoring a process with control charts, plots of subgroup statistics against limits (typically ±3 standard errors around the grand mean), to detect drift or shifts; a process whose points stay inside the limits is "in statistical control". *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="steady-state-response"></a>**Steady-state response** — The part of a stable linear system's response that remains after the transient decays, set by the input alone; for a sinusoidal input it is the phasor answer. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Transient](#transient).

<a id="step-response"></a>**Step response** — The response of a circuit to a source that switches from one constant value to another; for a first-order circuit, an exponential approach to the new final value. *First defined in* [07-02](../courses/07-circuit-analysis-2-transient-and-ac/chapters/07-02-first-order-rc-rl-transients.md).

<a id="stepping"></a>**Stepping** — A silicon revision of a chip (e.g., A0, A1, B0); commonly the number changes for metal-only revisions and the letter for full-layer revisions, though conventions vary. *First defined in* [00-05](../courses/00-orientation/chapters/00-05-how-chip-companies-are-organized.md).

<a id="stiff-system"></a>**Stiff system** — A system of differential equations whose time constants span many orders of magnitude, so explicit methods need steps set by the fastest one; circuit simulators therefore use implicit methods. *First defined in* [02-02](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-02-first-order-linear-odes.md). *See also:* [Euler's method](#eulers-method).

<a id="stokes-theorem"></a>**Stokes' theorem** — The circulation of a field around a closed loop equals the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by the loop; Green's theorem is its flat, two-dimensional case. *First defined in* [01-10](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-10-multivariable-calculus-2.md). *See also:* [Curl](#curl).

<a id="struct-padding"></a>**Struct padding** — Unused bytes a compiler inserts between and after struct fields so that each field is aligned to its size; field order changes a struct's size (uint8, uint32, uint16 is 12 bytes; uint32, uint16, uint8 is 8). *First defined in* [05-06](../courses/05-programming-for-engineers/chapters/05-06-c-pointers-and-memory.md).

<a id="student-t-distribution"></a>**Student t distribution** — The distribution of (X̄ − μ)/(S/√n) for Gaussian data, with n − 1 degrees of freedom; heavier-tailed than the Gaussian, so small-sample intervals use larger multipliers (2.776 for ν = 4 at 95%). *First defined in* [03-05](../courses/03-probability-statistics-and-random-variables/chapters/03-05-estimation-and-hypothesis-testing.md).

<a id="subspace"></a>**Subspace** — A subset of a vector space that contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, such as a line or plane through the origin, a column space or a null space. *First defined in* [02-07](../courses/02-complex-numbers-des-and-linear-algebra/chapters/02-07-determinants-inverses-and-vector-spaces.md).

<a id="substitution-integration"></a>**Substitution (integration)** — Evaluating ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx as ∫ f(u) du with u = g(x), the chain rule in reverse; for definite integrals the limits change to g(a) and g(b). *First defined in* [01-06](../courses/01-calculus-for-engineers/chapters/01-06-techniques-of-integration.md).

<a id="supermesh"></a>**Supermesh** — The loop around two meshes that share a current source, avoiding the source's branch; KVL around it does not involve the source's unknown voltage, and the source supplies the constraint i_a − i_b = ±I_s. *First defined in* [06-05](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-05-mesh-analysis.md). *See also:* [Supernode](#supernode), [Mesh analysis](#mesh-analysis).

<a id="supernode"></a>**Supernode** — A closed surface around a floating voltage source and its two nodes; KCL holds for the surface as a whole (the source's unknown current cancels), and the source supplies the constraint v_a − v_b = V_s. *First defined in* [06-04](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-04-nodal-analysis.md). *See also:* [Nodal analysis](#nodal-analysis).

<a id="superposition"></a>**Superposition** — In a linear circuit, any response to several independent sources equals the sum of the responses to each source acting alone, with the others switched off (voltage sources shorted, current sources opened) and dependent sources left in place. It does not apply to power. *First defined in* [06-07](../courses/06-circuit-analysis-1-dc/chapters/06-07-linearity-and-superposition.md). *See also:* [Linearity](#linearity), [Dependent source](#dependent-source).

<a id="superposition-electrostatics"></a>**Superposition (electrostatics)** — The principle that the field (or force) of many charges is the vector sum of their individual fields; for continuous charge the sum becomes an integral. *First defined in* [04-02](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-02-charge-coulomb-and-electric-fields.md).

<a id="surface-charge-density"></a>**Surface charge density** — Charge per unit area, σ (C/m²); on a conductor it is largest where the surface curves most sharply, and the field just outside is σ/ε₀. *First defined in* [04-03](../courses/04-physics-for-ee/chapters/04-03-gauss-law.md).
